title: Trace a fiber-optic prototype into live telephone service
question: Which design tested at Bell’s Atlanta facility went into Illinois Bell’s Chicago Lightwave trial, and when did the installation carry customer traffic?
summary: Bell Laboratories’ stacked-ribbon cable was ready for its complete Atlanta system test on 13 January 1976. Bell engineering reports describe the Chicago cable as a two-ribbon adaptation of Atlanta’s twelve-ribbon design. Independent confirmation of that design transfer is still open. Chicago’s cables were installed in February 1977. Illinois Bell fully cut over the trial system for customer traffic on 11 May 1977.
inputs: Prototype name and maker, technology designation and approximate year
Receiving operator, site, route endpoints and suspected operating window
Search variants for cable construction, terminal models and carrier bit rate
Existing discovery, event and source IDs for both endpoints

steps.title: Find the named systems
steps.action: Search discovery, source and lead files for the technology, prototype, operator and receiving-site aliases. Search original journal indexes and engineering archives for the prototype and operator or receiving city in the same query. Collect report titles from contents pages and follow the prototype and application papers cited by the receiving team.
steps.result: The dataset has early optical-fiber communication links and a generic research lead on operational low-loss optical fibre telephony. Searches for Atlanta Fiber System, Chicago Lightwave, Illinois Bell, fiber ribbon and adhesive sandwich found no record of this Atlanta cable adaptation. Searching the Bell Labs publications catalogue and Bell System Technical Journal for Atlanta Fiber System Experiment and Chicago Lightwave identified the July–August 1978 series. The Chicago paper’s opening points back to the Atlanta experiment and cable.

steps.title: Identify the demonstrated configuration
steps.action: In the prototype papers search for fabricated, test, demonstration, turn-up, interface and the model names. Read manufacturing and systems papers separately. Record the physical design, material supplier, test date, conditions and carried test signal. Inspect labelled cross sections and dated figures. Check what each date refers to before using it to date manufacture.
steps.result: Manufacturing drawings show twelve adhesive-sandwich ribbons of twelve Western Electric graded-index glass fibers in the protected core. The linear arrays supported group handling and splicing. Atlanta transmitted 44.7 Mb/s test signals through the complete simulated-plant system on 13 January 1976, bounding the cable’s manufacture. The loss comparison’s Atlanta Experiment – 1975 label does not identify a fabrication date. The M13 multiplex and D3 channel bank appear in the prototype report. The 144 nominal fiber positions exceeded the number of working fibers.

steps.title: Match the installed cable and terminals
steps.action: In the receiving operator’s engineering publication search the destination and prototype names alongside installation, splice, cable and the interface or terminal identifier. Match parts, alterations, date and route to drawings. Look for field measurements at the named route endpoints and note which parts were actually transferred, newly manufactured or never specified.
steps.result: The receiving paper explicitly traces the Chicago cable design to Atlanta and identifies its two-ribbon core. The new Bell Laboratories cables were installed on the Franklin–Wabash and Franklin–Brunswick legs in February 1977. The route and installed-medium measurements, plus a separate crosstalk study at the distributing frames, confirm actual installation of connectorized cable segments. The Chicago terminal diagram shows M13 multiplexes carrying DS3 at 44.7 Mb/s, with standard T1 input on the interoffice leg, SLC-40 customer terminals on the Brunswick leg, and added video encoding and decoding. The account describes shipment of much Atlanta equipment after modification, replacement or repackaging and supplies no component-by-component transfer list.

steps.title: Verify the operator’s service milestone
steps.action: Locate the operator’s annual reports or service bulletins for the trial year. Search inside for the project name, city, commercial service, cutover and traffic. Search digitized trade and local publications for the project or operator and date variants. Compare forecasts, installed status, customer traffic and full cutover by publication date and scope. Check whether a source quotes the developer or has its own reporting.
steps.result: The 1977 AT&T annual report states that it put the Chicago system in commercial service in May while it continued evaluation. It also prints an Illinois Bell executive’s statement about the 1977 installation. The engineering team dates full cutover to 11 May and names interoffice and customer voice, analog and digital data, and Picturephone Meeting Service. The September 1977 Electronic Design article independently publishes the same date and names the operator and services. Its reporting origins and any access to operator logs are unspecified. The engineering paper’s introductory claim of initial commercial traffic on 1 April differs from Hecht’s description of first test signals that day. The operator’s published month does not resolve the April accounts.

steps.title: Test the relationship against competing explanations
steps.action: Require explicit recipient attribution or a part-level match between maker and as-built installation, with chronology and distinct observations at both ends. Search contemporary trade archives, technical surveys and museum or company catalogues for both route names and the distinctive construction or part designation. Determine whether they document plans, reproduce the maker’s account or add an independent observation of the design that was installed. Classify the relationship using the dataset link vocabulary.
steps.result: Bell’s manufacturer and Chicago engineering reports describe the reduction from twelve ribbons to two. The crosstalk measurements record the installed configuration and share an author with the manufacturing report. A Canadian technical survey describes the planned Chicago ribbons as the same form as Atlanta’s. Radio-Electronics likewise describes a planned two-ribbon cable and names the earlier Atlanta test. These outside accounts leave the as-built design transfer unverified. Electronic Design corroborates service timing and the installed 24 fibers, with underlying reporting sources unknown. Similar optical loss, chronological succession and a shared DS3 rate alone would not identify the design origin.

decision: Keep a candidate adapts link from the tested Atlanta stacked-ribbon cable (13 January 1976) to the Chicago two-ribbon cable installation (February 1977), pending independent evidence of the as-built design transfer. Record Illinois Bell’s live trial use at full cutover on 11 May 1977. The character of the April traffic remains unresolved.
next: Look for a contemporary inspection or a catalogued Chicago cable sample with a construction record tied to the installed route. Search Illinois Bell engineering or operations records for April 1977 traffic authorization, a trunk cutover sheet or circuit logs before refining the first-live-traffic date.
reject_if: Reject a design transfer inferred only from shared materials, line rate, chronological proximity, a photograph or planned deployment. An announced test or installation without dated customer traffic does not establish live service. An annual report and a trade article repeating a project account are not automatically separate observations.
stop_when: Record an established link only when the maker and installed-system evidence identify the design and change and independent informative evidence corroborates the as-built transfer. If those sources are unavailable, retain a specific candidate and name the missing evidence. Record live use separately when a named operator or reliable contemporary witness identifies the service and its date or bounded window.
next_anchor: Apply this workflow to General Telephone of California’s Artesia–Long Beach link. Electronic Design, 1 September 1977, p. 107 names the GTE Laboratories developer, a T1 configuration and an April operating claim. Check the GTE engineering report and operating records independently, including whether publicity about another bit rate concerns that route and phase.
